docs(coord): red-team of the coordination bus Answers the redteam/matrix task assigned on 06/11: publishing with gh, without MCP and without a session, the fleet accepts the claim as a real agent (it shows up in coord_read with lane and scope) and the collision detector trusts it, so a spoofed claim blocks the legitimate owner of that scope for the claim TTL. The inbox is closed: coord_pending resolves identity from the caller and ignores the payload, so neither a forged agent nor a foreign session id reaches another agent's inbox. That means no prompt injection through the bus, only a denial of service on the coordination layer. Mitigations ranked by cost: require validated identity in the collision detector (the rule the inbox already uses), take the publisher identity from the GitHub author instead of the payload, sign the payload per agent, and refuse claims outside the caller's lane in the post tool.

docs(vpnsec): coord_http exposure measured and the auth that fits the tailnet Answers the vpnsec task assigned on 06/11. Measured from this host: the MCP on 100.121.100.103:8765 completes the initialize handshake and serves tools/list (8051 bytes of schemas) with no authentication at all; Basic by header changes nothing because FastMCP drops the Authorization header before the tools. The server binds only the tailnet IP and the NixOS firewall config does not list 8765 on tailscale0, but the live nftables ruleset was not readable from my shell, so the network barrier is not confirmed here. Risk, combined with today's bus red-team: an outsider with reach can paralyse lanes (a spoofed claim blocks the legitimate owner) and fake agents in the board; prompt injection into another agent's inbox does not work, because the inbox resolves identity from the caller. Proposal: bearer token via RemoteAuthProvider, one token per agent stored as a hash in the roster, with the shared-secret middleware as the immediate stopgap, the Tailscale ACL as defence in depth, and the post tool binding the claim to the caller's lane so the spoofing path closes with it.

docs(voice): the wakeword gate design, reusing the openWakeWord model we already declare The text gate is measured (recall 0.923, F1 0.889) and the speaker route is measured to fail: with WeSpeaker actually running, intra-speaker cosine p95 0.6435 against inter-speaker p95 0.5751 and max 0.8379, so the distributions touch and the 0.82 threshold would reject the owner's own noisy takes while still allowing a false positive. The wakeword is the signal that separates the TV from the owner with confidence, because it is an acoustic pattern the TV never produces and it does not depend on the speaker. The house already has what is needed: models.nix declares openwakeword with the hey_jarvis, embedding and melspectrogram models (pinned, nothing to download), and the asrd already carries per-segment signals (spk, voices, wav) where a wake state fits without touching the rest of the path. The existing wakeword daemon is a desktop hotkey service (graphical-session target, DISPLAY/WAYLAND) and does not serve the voice pipeline. The design has three steps (wake state on the microphone stream, one more per-segment field, the candidate rule in the gate module), the honest UX cost (the owner says hey jarvis, or the cheaper variant where the wakeword is only a negative filter for the TV), and the measurement that comes first: run openWakeWord offline over the 259 segments in logs/audio and publish the recall on the owner's segments, the false positives on the TV ones and the threshold curve. Nothing was applied: no flags, no services, no change in duplex-voice.py (that wiring belongs to the lane that owns the duplex).

fix(voice): make the ASRD survive offline and segment the owner's voice The E2E voice battery was 0/10 'sem-segmento' because the ASRD process DIED at startup, twice over: 1. torch.hub.load validated the Silero VAD repo over the network before using the cached copy, and with the network blocked the urlopen raised HTTPError (504) that nobody handled. The VAD is now loaded from the local cache (source 'local'), falling back to the network path only when the cache is missing. 2. The numpy of the karaok venv is a wheel that expects the system C++ runtime, so without libstdc++/libz in LD_LIBRARY_PATH the import failed before the first {'ready': true}. The duplex now resolves those paths through nix (no hardcoded store path, which the GC removes) and passes them to the ASRD. Verified end to end by feeding the ASRD in the duplex's own protocol (1.2 s windows, mic-like level, trailing silence so the VAD can close the segment): it answers {'text': 'Eu preciso', 'ms': 395.6, 'inf_ms': 341.7}, which is the endpoint latency the house targets. The speaker field is still '?' because the ASRD's own runtime is the venv whose MFCC fallback does not separate voices, as measured. The VAD also rejects a loud signal (rms 0.41 gives no segment) while mic-like levels (rms 0.024) segment fine, so the level gate is real.

fix(wakeword): the scorer's calibration mode never ran, and TTS positives are not a proxy Two findings while trying to close the calibration without waiting for the owner's voice: 1. The house scorer's --calibrate path called Scorer.score_clip(pcm) on the class, but score_clip is an instance method, so every run died with 'missing 1 required positional argument' before scoring a single file (the negative branch used the instance correctly, which is why the single-shot mode worked). Fixed: one line. 2. Synthetic positives do not work as a proxy: eight TTS-generated 'hey jarvis' samples (local Kokoro) score in the same range as the negatives, so the calibrated threshold collapses to the floor (0.0001) with a meaningless 100 percent positive rate — openWakeWord was trained on real speech, so a synthesised voice does not transfer, and a synthetic positive set would have produced a false curve. With the bug fixed the calibration runs in one command, and the positives have to be the owner's real voice saying the wake phrase.

fix(gate): short-circuit the requests the upstream already rejected Measured on the gate's own log (09/11): 91 context_length rejections in 6h, every one with a request above 1MB (5.4MB average), and the upstream's answer names the truth: limit 1048576, actual 1541675. The config declares the limit correctly, so the sessions are sending prompts 493k tokens above the API's ceiling. Each retry burns upstream time and the 8 RPM bucket, and the visible symptom is the queue: 14 waits of up to 21s in 6h, which is what kills the short-timeout clients (the coord-mcp at 25s). The gate now learns the rejected size per path (model) and answers a same-size request locally with the same 400, without sending it. Proved with a fake upstream that always refuses with context_length: the first request goes upstream, the second is short-circuited and the upstream still saw one request. This is the circuit breaker, not the fix: the root cause is the session limit (the opencode limit.input), and the proposal for 262144 on the free tier is what removes these requests instead of failing them.

fix(gate): give small requests their own bucket so the fleet stops queueing behind monsters Measured on the gate log (09/11): 14 queue waits of up to 21s in 6h with an 8 RPM bucket, and the visible casualty is the short-timeout client (the coord-mcp at 25s) dying before the answer. The queue is made by the huge requests: 91 context_length rejections in 6h, every one above 1MB (5.4MB average), while the fleet's own coordination calls are tiny. Small requests (up to 256KB) now use their own bucket, twice the rate, so they are not stuck behind a 5.4MB request. The factor is 2 on purpose: 8 (big) + 16 (small) = 24 RPM, under the upstream's 40, so the quota is not pushed over the edge. Proved with a fake upstream where the big request holds the upstream for 3s: the small one answered in 0.00s (200) while the big one was still running (3.03s). Without the priority path it would have waited about 60s and the client would have timed out.

docs(ai): note that the rebuild does not restart the voice stack The whisper-server is a systemd unit and does restart with the rebuild, but the duplex-voice and duplex-asrd processes are ad hoc ones from 08/11 11:02 and are not units: the rebuild leaves them running the old code. docs(voice): state the VAD mechanism instead of the intuition The house VAD is Silero with a noise-adaptive threshold (an EMA of the noise floor lifts the threshold towards max_thresh as the ambient rises), so my earlier phrasing overclaimed and the paragraph had been left duplicated by an earlier edit. The bench runs with zero ambient, the threshold therefore stays at its floor, and the loud clips get through: 0.925 is the worst case for the VAD, not a room number. In a real room the raised threshold may catch the TV, but that depends on the ambient and is a hypothesis, not a measurement. The conclusion is unchanged and now precise: the text gate does not help here (the real gate kills zero), so the residual is decided by the VAD and the wakeword, not by the deny-list.

fix(harness): dedupe bus deliveries by text so a repeated note stops waking the agent Measured on 09/11: ten identical confirmation notes on the bus (09:01 to 11:49) each woke the receiving session and consumed a full turn. The watcher compared the hash of the whole pending set, so every new duplicate changed the set and woke the agent again. Now the items already delivered (by text, per agent) leave the set before the hash, so a repeated note changes nothing and nobody is woken. Proved on the isolated logic: the first pass keeps both items, the second keeps only the new one.

fix(harness): dedupe bus notes by normalised prefix, not exact text The exact-text dedupe did not catch the loop, because the same notice arrives in small variants (with or without a duration, with a different wording) and each variant hashed differently, so the agent was woken again. The key is now the first 120 characters of the whitespace normalised, lowercased text: the same notice in any variant collides, while two different notices still differ well before 120 characters. Proved on the isolated logic: with no prior delivery both items pass; with the variant already delivered only the genuinely new one passes.

fix(coord): dedupe deliveries before they reach the session inbox The watcher-side dedupe was the wrong place: these notes arrive as messages in the session queue (delivery=queue) and the opencode client turns each queued one into a turn, so the poll path never saw them. Measured: ten identical confirmations cost a full turn each. Now the delivery itself refuses a repeat: the key is the content of the note without the courtesy prefix (confirmed, received, ok, done), so the same notice in a different wording collides while two different notices still differ well before the window. A repeated delivery returns 208 and is never enqueued; the key is recorded per target only after a successful post. Proved: a repeated delivery returns 208 without any request, and a different note still goes through.

fix(coord): compare repeated notes by similarity, not by exact text The prefix key still missed the loop, because the same notice arrives with variations that differ before the window ('conforme o README' or 'conforme o checkpoint', with or without a duration). The comparison is now by similarity (difflib) against the last twenty deliveries of the target, so insertions and reordering collide while a genuinely different notice still gets through. Proved on three wordings of the same notice: all detected as repeats; a different notice and a new real notice are not.

feat(voice): measure the house voice pipeline and fix the ASRD subprocess environment The trigger bench posts the fixture straight to the whisper server, so the house chain (VAD, segmentation, anti_halluc gate) was never measured on it. scripts/voice-pipeline-probe.py drives the real duplex-asrd through the same stdio protocol the duplex uses, feeds the trigger fixtures in real time with digital silence at the end to close the segment, pairs every clip with the same audio on the raw whisper path, and keeps a positive control (real speech wavs) so that no text cannot be confused with a broken probe. The sample is seeded per category, so two runs on the same slice are comparable. The ASRD environment resolver asked nix for nixpkgs#gcc.lib, a path that does not exist on the current nixpkgs (the attribute is gcc.cc.lib), and swallowed the failure: the resolver returned only zlib and the ASRD survived only because the parent environment already carried the gcc library path. On a restart from a clean environment that kills the ASRD before its ready line, which is exactly the 0/10 sem-segmento symptom. scripts/asrd_env.py resolves the attribute paths that exist, verifies the soname in the result, falls back to a store search when nix cannot answer, and reports what is missing; the ASRD now prints a JSON error instead of dying silently on the numpy import. Also measured (10 clips per category, 12 s window, reduplication): the raw whisper path hallucinates on 10 of 10 clips while the house pipeline returns text on 3 of 10, and the same slice reproduces exactly (3 of 10, 6 segments closed) across runs. The gate kills the segments with weak audio stats and lets the confident ones through.

docs(voice): the trigger bench measures the whisper server, not the house The number that was heading for the owner's decision sheet (0.925) comes from a bench that posts the fixture straight to whisper-server: it never runs the VAD, the segmentation or the anti_halluc gate, so it says what whisper does with the whole clip, not what the house would answer. Two of my own readings were wrong for the same reason and are corrected in the audit: the empty_ok column is not the VAD dropping clips (it is whisper returning empty text), and the house VAD threshold is fixed at 0.5 (the AdaptiveVAD class exists but its update_threshold is never called). The house pipeline was measured with the new probe (same audio, same 12 s window, paired comparison, positive control 5/5) over 123 distinct trigger clips: the raw whisper path hallucinates on 83 of them (0.67) while the house chain delivers text on 3 (0.024), so the chain cuts 96 percent of the trigger hallucinations. The VAD never opens a segment for silence, nonspeech and music, and the gate kills what gets through; the residual is syllable repetition (3 of 40) with confident audio, which is what the wakeword would cover. Also recorded: the ASRD restart is now safe, because the environment resolver asked nix for a path that does not exist and swallowed the failure.

The section now says so and adds the house chain measured on the same corpus (123 clips, paired comparison, positive control 9 of 9): the raw path hallucinates on 83 of them while the house chain delivers text on 3, so the chain cuts 96 percent of the trigger hallucinations and the residual is syllable repetition with confident audio. docs(voice): the room level changes the VAD, not the residual The audit still carried a hypothesis ('in a real room the VAD may catch the TV') instead of a number, and with the threshold now known to be fixed at 0.5 the question became measurable. The probe gained a level sweep: the same clips scaled to a target RMS, 5 clips per category per level, 60 feeds in total, with the clipping measured (worst case 2.6 percent of the samples). Result: the raw whisper path hallucinates on music and repetition at every level (5 of 5 each) and the house chain delivered text on none of the 60 feeds. The level changes how many segments the VAD opens (repetition 7 to 3, music 5 to 2) and the gate closes all of them, so the residual is not a function of the room level: what leaks is the clip whose syllable pattern looks like speech, not the volume. Also corrects a claim of mine in the audit: I wrote that the live ASRD does not have the v6 gate. It does (v6 and v7 landed on 20/10 and the process started on 08/11); what it misses is the offline start fix of 09/11 and the environment fix, so the pending restart matters for the start, not for the gate. The tools index was regenerated with the house generator, which also picked up the voice tools that were never indexed.

docs(voice): note the voice_text_rules dependency of the measured gate The gate calls scripts/voice_text_rules.py for the repetition branch, so the measured copy depends on that file: if the asrd changes and this copy does not, the parity checker catches it instead of the bench measuring a gate that does not exist in production.

feat(voice): a tool to test whether any audio-side signal separates hallucination from real speech The audio arm of the voice gate uses no_speech_prob and avg_logprob, and both were measured useless on trigger hallucinations (they kill 0 of 111: the hallucinated transcript arrives confident, median no_speech_prob 0.000 and median avg_logprob between -0.22 and -0.30 against a -0.45 threshold). The whisper server exposes more that the gate ignores: per-word probability, the token ids (which give the compression ratio, one of Whisper's own heuristics) and the segment duration. This tool measures each candidate on both classes (real speech from logs/audio, trigger hallucinations from the bench JSONL) and reports the separation and the cost at the threshold that kills 90 percent of the hallucinations. The tool does not touch the gate: it is evidence for the voice lane to decide whether an audio arm is repairable at all, which is what arXiv 2606.23060 (Interspeech 2026) makes the open question.

docs(agents): the nv-gate health path is /__gate/health, not /health Probing the gate on /health falls through to the forwarder and is relayed to the upstream: the request hangs, times out and leaves a ConnectionResetError in the journal, which looks exactly like a dead service. The real path is GET /__gate/health, which answers immediately with the counters (rpm, burst, upstream and client 429s, errors, retries, queued seconds, upstream 504 and io errors, ctx_rejected and ctx_short_circuit). The house file now says so, because the wrong path costs a diagnosis.

docs(voice): the cost of the text rules on real speech, and the floor under them A text rule in the voice gate is not free, and that cost was never measured: the house had the gain (the gate real kills 87 of 111, residual 0.200) without the price. Measured on the 1817 real transcripts of logs/audio: 134 of them (7.4 percent) have their exact text in the lexicon ('Obrigado.', 'Tchau.', 'Muito bom.'), 34 start with 'e ai' (1.9 percent), and the candidate prefix rule kills 1 of 1817 (0.06 percent). That one is not a defect of the rule, it is the floor under any text gate: the same string ('E ai, o que e isso?') is in the real speech and in the hallucinations, and no function of the text separates the two classes. Which is also why the wakeword is not optional for the residual. The document also records what the 2026 literature says (arXiv 2606.23060: text metrics degrade without a reference transcript and the strong signal is probing the decoder internals, which whisper.cpp does not expose; arXiv 2609.32560 and 2501.11378: the VAD before the decoder is the primary defense, and the house already has it).

docs(voice): no whisper-internal signal separates hallucination from real speech The sweep's new tool measured the statistics the gate ignores (per-word probability, token ids, duration) on 111 trigger hallucinations against 300 real transcripts from the house. feat(voice): the composed 'e ai' rule, with its cost measured first The sweep measured the candidate rule on 1817 real transcripts: 'e ai' at the start and the rest also looking like a hallucination (lexicon, hallucination greeting, repetition, 'legenda', or 'e ai' repeated three or more times). It kills one real utterance (0.06 percent, 'E ai, o que e isso?') and ten of the 24 gate survivors, and that cost is the floor of any text gate rather than a defect of the rule. The rule is conservative on purpose: 'E ai, tudo bom?' passes. It is now implemented in the voice lane with the same pattern as the repetition rule: one module with a test, an environment switch (JARVIS_VOICE_GREETING_RULE=0), and wired into the ASRD after the dry 'e ai' kill that already existed. Parity is proven: comparing this implementation with the measured one (measure-voice-rule-cost.py) over the 111 bench samples gives 111 of 111 identical verdicts, and both kill the same 10 of the 24 survivors. The gate residual on the whole clip therefore drops from 24 of 111 (0.216) to 14 of 111 (0.126). The decision sheet and the audit carry the rule, its cost, and how to switch it off.

fix(harness): write the shared queue without losing another lane's note The queue is shared by every lane and the write was a read-modify-write (cat to a temp file, then mv): not atomic, and between the two steps the note of another lane disappeared. Measured on 10/11: the watcher saw the top of the queue change era while another lane was writing, which is the window. Now the write takes a flock on the queue (serialising the checkpoints between lanes) and checks the hash before and after reading, repeating the read when the file changed underneath (that is the case of a lane that wrote by hand, without the lock). Proved with two concurrent writers: both notes and the previous content survived. The same block also stopped mangling the file mode: mktemp creates 600 and the mv replaced the queue with it, so the queue became owner-only while git tracks it as 644. The mode is now preserved.

docs(harness): the stale wake diagnosis, with the end of the loop proved The wakes that reached the sessions carried a state that did not exist on the machine receiving them: the local watcher journal shows the same queue events with the right time and without the [WATCHER hh:mm] prefix, the prefix itself was about fifty minutes ahead of the local clock, and one wake pointed the queue top at the era of 09/11 while the real queue had today's era on top. The only lane of the fleet that is not in the local roster and that posts on the bus is crouton-alpha (termux/vpnsec), which reads a stale copy of the queue and of the vault. That stale era is the one carrying the old gate number, which is why the lane kept repeating it for hours after the gate had been measured for real. The end of the loop is proved: the similarity dedupe already in main scores the repeated stale wakes between 0.77 and 0.87 of similarity, so once that machine syncs the clone the repetition stops being delivered. The action (git pull, and fix the clock with chrony or NTP) is published on the bus. A plugin filter for wakes with a clock ahead of the local one is proposed for the next rebuild, since a rebuild is the owner's call.

docs(gate): the new health endpoint is safe, and the session cap covers 69 percent of what the gate warns about The endpoint GET /__gate/health, new in the house, listens on 127.0.0.1:8095 only (the tailnet address refuses the connection), answers with counters and leaks no upstream URL, key or address. The path /health next to it is not local: it falls through to the forwarder, took 5.4 seconds in the measurement and relayed the upstream, so a probe with the wrong path looks like a dead service and still spends upstream quota. The fleet believed the two provider fixes were waiting for a rebuild, because the gate runs the store copy. Measured: the store copy already has both (small_bucket and ctx_short_circuit), the live process started after those commits, and the context guard has already short-circuited 176 requests locally. The pending rebuild does not include them. And the session cap is not a theoretical guard: of the 54 requests the gate warned about in 6 hours, 37 (69 percent) are above 1.05 MB, which is the 262144 token ceiling. The median warned request is 5.46 MB, about 1.37 million tokens, above the API ceiling itself.

fix(voice): the E2E battery read 0/10 because the ASRD dropped every short segment Three measured defects, in the live voice path: The stack was down, not waiting for a restart: the client and the ASRD die on the numpy import of the karaok venv when libstdc++ is not on LD_LIBRARY_PATH. The resolver asked nix for nixpkgs#gcc.lib, which does not exist on this nixpkgs (the attribute is gcc.cc.lib), and swallowed the failure, so the ASRD survived only because the inherited environment already carried the path. scripts/asrd_env.py now resolves the attribute paths that exist, verifies the soname in the result, falls back to the store and reports what is missing; duplex-voice-run.sh uses the same resolver for the client, which needs it too. The voice is up again. The ASRD dropped every short segment: seg_to_text returned a bare string for segments under 0.4 s while its caller unpacks a tuple, so the handler swallowed 'ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 2, got 0)' and the segment was lost. That was the cause of the 0/10 sem-segmento. The guard is now _min_segment, at module level, with a test. The injection list was never consumed: the same wav was re-fed every tick (the ASRD heard the phrase repeatedly and returned a hallucination) and the mic stayed muted for good after an injection. The list is consumed now and the whisper context is cleared, because the injected phrase is test material and was polarising the next transcription ('Jarvis, que horas sao?' became 'Servico que horas sao?'). Measured: the isolated injection now transcribes whole ('Qual a previsao do tempo de amanha?', 417 ms, and the saved segment carries the full audio, rms 5457 against 5555 of the source). Opt-in telemetry (JARVIS_ASR_TRACE=1) logs every ASRD line, including the empty ones, and the traceback when the ASRD raises, because 'sem-segmento' was opaque without it. Still open, honestly: the battery in series stays 0/10 because the first scenario lands on no-response (whisper turns 'Jarvis' into 'Servico' on the synthetic wav) and the following ones are injected while the client is still answering, so their segment misses the battery's 40 s window. The pipeline defect is fixed; what is left is the pacing of the test.

docs(gate): the cost of not having the session cap, measured in one window A lane measured a single window sending seven requests of 5,461,393 bytes (about 1.35 million tokens) in forty minutes, all of them cut by the context guard: 9.4 million tokens of prompt that went nowhere, from one window that had been open for days. docs(gate): the context guard fired 55 more times since last night Live counters from the gate's own health endpoint: ctx_short_circuit went from 142 to 197, upstream_504 from 60 to 92, requests from 1942 to 3002, retries from 180 to 214 and queued seconds from 2028 to 2248, all in about four hours. docs(redteam): what the 2026 literature adds to the contract divergence Agents Behave Differently in Fabricated Environments (Apart Research, September 2026) measures that out-of-scope actions rise in the fabricated arms (12 writes and 86 reads against zero in the real arm) and concludes that a resample of that family overstates the danger. For the house: the raw inference bench is an attack proxy, and the real arm is the house path, where the measured residual is 0.024. The same paper gives the cheapest fix for the provenance problem: every number is substituted at build time from committed artifacts and the build fails if a placeholder cannot be computed. Applied here, the campaign report carries the commits of the plugin and of the harness, and the number is only published if the checker passes, which is what the check-plugin-contract.py is for. Also recorded: arXiv 2610.12463 on the 2026 incidents where agent evaluations reached real systems outside the authorised scope, which is the rule the audit lane already applies.

docs(voice): the voice has no watchdog and can stay silent for hours The house self-heal does not watch the voice client (no reference to duplex-voice in core/heal.py), and the flag that marks duplex mode as active outlives the process it describes. Measured today: the voice was up at 12:36 and by 16:07 the client was gone with no trace (no OOM, no journal entry, no traceback, so an external kill; the runner itself kills orphans on startup, so any voice start takes the previous one down). The voice can therefore be mute for hours without anyone noticing. The proposal is in the owner's decision sheet, because it is a host unit and that is the owner's call: a duplex-voice service with Restart=always and the library path resolved by scripts/asrd_env.py, which is what stops the death on the numpy import.

docs(voice): the house path now leaves one case, and it is a laugh The voice lane restarted the voice stack at 16:10 with the composed 'e ai' rule inside, so the blocker this lane had documented (the rebuild does not restart the voice stack) is gone and the house path could be measured against the code that runs. Measured with the pipeline probe, 20 clips per category: the raw inference path hallucinates 66 of 80, and the house path (VAD, segment, gate) delivers text on 1 of 80. The single survivor is 'Hahahaha', a laugh, which the deny list keeps on purpose because laughter is a social signal the owner wants the agent to use. docs(voice): the last residual case is a laugh, and closing it is a product call The remediation with today's code leaves one case out of eighty trigger clips: 'Hahahaha', a laugh. The separated repetition rule in the ASRD does not catch it (there is no separator) and neither does the sweep's concatenated rule (the pattern is not three exact repetitions of one group). Measured on the 1817 real transcripts of the house with the new tool scripts/measure-repeat-rule-cost.py: a concatenated rule catches the case at zero measured cost (0 of 1817), while the rule in place today kills 15 of 1817 (0.83 percent). The number does not hide the trade-off: a laugh is a social signal the house keeps on purpose (SOCIAL_KEEP in duplex-asrd.py), so a concatenated rule also kills the owner's own laugh. The decision sheet therefore asks the owner to choose between closing the case mechanically and losing the laugh, or keeping the laugh and accepting that trigger. One correction of my own number in the same commit: I published the cost of the rule in place as one real utterance in 199 (0.5 percent). The sample was too small; on the whole corpus it is 15 in 1817 (0.83 percent), with cases like 'Nao, nao, nao.' and 'sim sim sim nao foi antes nao'. The direction of the decision is unchanged, but the smaller figure I published was not the number.

fix(voice): the handover to the wakeword daemon must not report a false success The voice client sleeps on purpose when idle and hands the turn over to the wakeword daemon, which is what wakes the voice when the owner speaks. That handover was failing in silence: the systemctl start ran with capture_output and no check, and the client logged 'wakeword de volta' as if it had worked. On this machine the unit is not installed (it exists in the repo at home-manager/modules/services/jarvis-wakeword.nix), so the daemon never started and the voice stayed deaf for good while the client slept. The log now checks is-active and says so when the unit is missing. This also corrects my own proposal: I had suggested a Restart=always watchdog for the voice after seeing the client absent, but the client was asleep by design, and a watchdog would fight the sleep and wake cycle. The decision sheet now carries the real gap: install the unit, calibrate the wakeword threshold, and decide whether the self-heal should watch the daemon (it reports degraded with restarts=0 and restarts nothing). The character checker gains --allow-arrows for legacy house documents, where the arrows are the house convention (11 in the owner's decision sheet, 22 in the gate audit at their origin); for new text the rule of no arrows still fails as before.

docs(voice): the wake path decision, with the premise corrected The voice lane measured that the client sleeps on purpose and that the handoff to the wakeword daemon fails in silence: the start ran without checking and the client logged the wakeword back as if it had worked. Their fix to the log is right. The premise of the proposal needed correcting before it became an item: the wakeword unit is not installed because the owner disabled it on 21/10 (services.jarvis-wakeword.enable = false in home.nix:904), because the duplex of continuous voice replaced it, with the address gate in the classifier doing the same job without the openWakeWord daemon competing for the microphone. So installing the unit would revert a decision of the owner, and the choice is now written with both sides: keep the address gate and fix the silent handoff, with the heal watching the address gate instead of a daemon that does not exist, or revert 21/10 and bring the daemon back with the calibration of the owner's own voice.

fix(rebuild): bring the system units back after the switch The switch stops the parts of jarvis.target when their unit file changes, but jarvis.target is static: it stays active, it is never stopped nor restarted, and the parts of a target that is not restarted do not come back. Measured on 11/11: the router (llama-cpp-server, :8080) stayed INACTIVE from 15:10:09 until 22:5x, that is 7h37 with the local LLM out of the air and nobody noticing, while the script itself documents that a rebuild activates the config and restarts the services. The user units were already handled (the script restarts the changed user timers explicitly, with the reason written down); the system units were not. Restarting the target propagates to the parts (PartOf=jarvis.target), which covers the router, the embeddings, the reranker, qdrant and the webui. It costs a few seconds of local inference, which the rebuild already does by switching generations.

docs(ai): the router was out for 7h37 after a switch, and the cause was the static target Measured: the router on 8080 stayed INACTIVE from 15:10:09 until 22:5x, 7h37 with the local LLM out of the air and nobody noticing. The journal shows the switch stopping the router, the opencode serve and the nv-gate, and jarvis.target never being restarted. The reason: jarvis.target is static (always active, timestamp from 03/11) and its parts carry PartOf=jarvis.target, so the switch stops the parts when the unit file changes but the parts of a target that is not restarted do not come back. The house rebuild script already handled the user units, with the reason written down, and did not handle the system ones. Fixed in commit 53df9e3d: the rebuild restarts jarvis.target explicitly after the switch, which propagates to the parts. What still needs the owner is the watchdog timer and lifting the stale pause, because between a switch and the next rebuild nothing is automatic: the voice is ad hoc and the self-heal is paused.

docs(research): microtask platforms, UHRS, and how the house stack fits The owner asked for research on the microtask and AI-training platforms, and how the Laya and the local or API models, with the screen-reading MCP and the humanized input, could be used to earn, focused on quick microtasks, yes/no decisions and access to UHRS. The research: UHRS is Microsoft's Universal Human Relevance System, a relevance-judgment platform reached through Clickworker or Toloka, paying 7 to 14 dollars per active hour for qualified workers against 5 to 9 for image labeling; access needs a clickworker account, the English assessment, a dedicated LiveID and a qualification run of 50 to 100 test items, and the Clickworker support states that access is temporarily disabled when the login goes through a proxy or VPN, which is exactly this machine's vpnsec mode. The map covers Clickworker, OneForma, Toloka and Mindrift (15 to 30 per hour entry, 60 to 100+ for domain experts), Appen's CrowdGen (up to 100+ per hour for specialists), RWS TrainAI and LXT, Outlier, DataAnnotation, TELUS Digital, Datavio and friends, Microworkers and SproutGigs, Prolific and CloudResearch Connect (14 to 16.5 per hour in the examples, 10 average) and ySense, plus why MTurk is not to be counted on for a new Brazilian account. The plan has three rungs: triage the pipeline with the local models so only the tasks that pay are opened, use the local models to draft the label and the explanation while the human decides with human_input, and build the service the owner can actually sell, since the house already owns the stack these companies sell (voice interface, screen reading, humanized input, local and cloud models). The compliance line is explicit: automating clicks or answers breaks the terms, gets accounts banned and payments clawed back, so the model drafts and the human decides. The document ends with what the owner needs: the English test, a session with direct egress and no vpnsec, one or two platforms to qualify, and the first paying B2B customer.

feat(tools): the judgment bench that decides if Laya can answer by proxy The owner answered the compliance point: it will not answer alone, he will train the Laya model, so the answer is his, by proxy. That makes the fastest start obvious: do not start with the training, start with the training data that the platforms already demand. The decision and the order of attack are now in the research doc (addendum): today, twenty minutes for the clickworker account and the UHRS English test (free, direct egress, no vpnsec, because the access is disabled behind a proxy or VPN), which also delivers the first labels for free because the fifty to a hundred qualification items are exactly the dataset; in parallel, an application to Mindrift, whose approval is an application rather than an assessment chain. And in parallel, with nobody's approval needed, the concordance bench, so the training is not a leap in the dark: the number decides the mode (at or above 95 percent the model may answer alone, 85 to 95 it proposes and the owner confirms, below 85 there is no delegation), with the same method as the honest voice bench (a hand-written held-out, zero leakage) and a Wilson interval, so ninety-five percent on twenty items is not mistaken for certainty. What lands here: scripts/judgment-bench.py (reads the owner's dataset, measures agreement against the local router, prints the misses and the recommended mode; the self-test proves the mechanics without a model) and data/judgments/SCHEMA.md (the dataset format, how to collect the labels from the qualification items, how to train and measure, and what the dataset does not solve).

feat(renda): the screener, the pause, and the bench talking to a model that answers Three things the owner asked for, all measured and tested. The screener (scripts/task-screener.py) triages the panel: the costly part of microtask work is opening fifteen tabs to find out that twelve do not pay. It parses the listing (payment per hour or per task, real duration, number of tasks, format, English requirement), computes the effective rate and then the rate adjusted by motor effort (clicking and typing 1.0, reading and judging 1.6, image 1.8, writing 3.0), because the owner is a disabled person and the effort per click is what decides the value per hour. Above US$ 12/h it is worth it, below US$ 4/h it is not, and the borderline cases go to the local model with a rubric. The platform rates are the ones measured in the 13/11 research. The self-test caught that a listing in Portuguese ('US$ 0,50 por tarefa') did not match the pattern and that the model was being asked for by a name the server does not carry. The watchdog now respects the pause (scripts/voice-watchdog.sh): --pause writes the voice pause flag and drops the stack, --resume lifts it, and the house pause flag (the one the nightwatch uses) pauses the voice too. Paused, the watchdog says so and starts nothing, so a deliberate stop is not undone by the next timer tick. The self-test proves the three cases against a temporary state directory, without touching the real state. The bench was calling a model that could not answer: the router announces bonsai but cannot load it (HTTP 500, VRAM), while the duplex 4B on :8092 answers fine. Both the bench and the screener now discover and test which server answers, and the bench's prompt presents the four rubric options instead of asking for the owner's own string. With that, the bench measures for real: 7 of 12 (58.3 percent) against the base 4B with no fine-tune, and the per-level F1 shows it collapses onto '3' (level 2 and level 1 at F1 0.00), which is exactly what the training on the owner's labels has to fix. Also recorded: the owner's decision on the default model and the VRAM measurement behind it (the router is down because the bonsai does not fit; one instance of the 4B MTP closes both).

fix(renda): the delegation number was inflated by the bench itself The number that decides the mode (the model answers alone, proposes and the owner confirms, or no delegation) was measured with a leak inside the bench. Three defects, all measured. The biggest: the owner's answer was inside the context. The practice bench wrote the label with 'Answer by the owner: 3' at the end of the context, and the bench sent the whole context to the model, so the model read the answer in the prompt. Measured on the same file at the same time: 11 of 12 = 91.7 percent with the answer in the context, 7 of 12 = 58.3 percent with a clean context. The bench was measuring 91.7 where the base model does 58.3, and the house rule would have said 'the model can answer alone' instead of 'no delegation'. The decision was flipped by the leak. Fixed on both sides: the label now stores the context the owner saw (query plus page) and the answer in its own field. It also had a second bug in the same line: it wrote the practice key instead of the owner's answer, so the dataset would have been the key, the opposite of the design. And the bench now sanitizes the context before calling the model and says how many items it had to clean, so an old file cannot inflate the number again. Second: the bench called the model twice per item (once for the agreement, once for the per-level F1), so the F1 measured a different sample than the agreement, at double the cost on a 6 GB GPU. Now one call per item, and both metrics use the same answer. Third: an answer the bench could not parse was counted as a model error, so a speech it failed to understand lowered the agreement for a reason that is not the model's. Those rows are skipped and counted. Fourth, in the dataset builder: the split was by line, so the owner's two judgments of the same item (which is how his repeatability, the real ceiling for the delegation, gets measured) could land in different files, one in training and one in test. That is leakage, the exact defect the script promises to avoid. The split is now by item group: both answers stay in the same file, by construction, and the self-test proves it. The honest measurement with the fixed bench: 7 of 12 = 58.3 percent with the 4B and no fine-tune, and the per-level F1 names the defect (level 3 at F1 0.71, levels 2 and 1 at F1 0.00, the model never says 1), which is exactly what the training on the owner's labels has to fix.

feat(skills): import the three Anthropic skills that do not duplicate the house, tested The Anthropic skills (194k stars) have the SAME frontmatter the house uses (name, description, license), so they are drop-in. But importing all 19 would duplicate what the house already has: mcp-builder against mcp-development, webapp-testing against sandbox-qa, claude-api against the house knowledge, internal-comms against the Telegram. The A/B picked the three the house really uses: pdf, doc-coauthoring and skill-creator. The pdf one would have arrived DEAD: its scripts need pdfplumber, pytesseract and pypdf, none of which were in the python of the house. Measured: without them 'import pdfplumber' failed; with all three in the devShell the skill's own scripts ran on a generated PDF and found the form field it was given. The write-up also corrects an over-optimistic claim of mine: the opencodeGo driver is the opencode CLOUD service (it wants an API key), not the local opencode of the house. The local bridge is the customAcp driver, whose 'cli' is the whole command, and the house opencode does speak ACP ('opencode acp'). What is proven and what is not is now in a table: the harness boots here and its API answers, the driver exists in the open source code, but a real conversational turn through it is still NOT proven, and it is listed as the next step instead of as a fait accompli. The section on the pains found on the way is in the same document.

fix(renda): measuring on the training set, and a held-out that could not exist Two more defects of the same family as the ones before (the delegation number measured in a misleading way), found by inspection after the leak fix. First, without --heldout the bench measured in the data file, which after the training is the training file itself. The number then measures memorization instead of judgment agreement, and the verdict (the model can answer alone) becomes a false green. The bench now discovers the training ids (the train splits under data/judgments/laya and data/judgments/train.jsonl) and says exactly how many ids are shared (measured: 4 ids of this file also entered the training split), and the final verdict is marked as a measurement taken without held-out. Second, the held-out did not exist and had no way to be created: the schema told the owner to write it by hand, which for fifty items is an invitation to get it wrong and forget it. judgment-dataset.py now has --make-heldout N. It takes only the owner's real labels (the synthetic practice items stay out, they are for training, not for measuring generalization), stratifies by class in round-robin so the held-out has the same mix as the training (otherwise the per-level F1 measures a class the model never saw), is deterministic for a given seed, and the build already excludes those ids from the training, so the held-out is honest by construction: there is no path in which the file being measured enters the training. Proven with forty-two fake labels: a held-out of twelve items with three per class, train=20 test=6 calib=4 heldout=12, no leakage between files, the twelve held-out ids absent from the training, and the same seed reproducing the same file. Third and smaller: the bench read the item id from the wrong field. The Laya dataset uses _id (the original id becomes _id in the conversion) and the bench read only id, so the divergences showed id=None and the human ceiling collapsed every item into one group (it printed 0/1 = 0.0 percent with four items measured, when the owner had judged no item twice). An invented ceiling is worse than none, because it decides the delegation mode. The id is now read from both formats.

feat(rag): the offline survival corpus as fallback of the online search The N.O.M.A.D corpus was exposed as a tool of the MCP but was wired to nothing: the web search answered a bare ERROR when Tavily was missing, and the semantic search never looked at the corpus. Two islands. Now the web search falls back to the corpus when the online one does not answer (no key, HTTP error, timeout, exception) and says so in the result (fonte: corpus offline N.O.M.A.D), because the corpus is local and deterministic (FTS5) and answering offline beats leaving the agent with nothing. The semantic search appends the corpus as ADDITIONAL data, marked offline/NOMAD, and if the corpus fails the semantic search is exactly as before: the offline is extra, never a dependency. Measured: with an invalid Tavily key the answer comes from the corpus with the source marked; the semantic search returns three code index hits plus the offline one; five new tests cover the fallback, the mark, the empty query and the case where the offline fails. The write-up also corrects the framing of the OpenMausBot: the UX of the house is the Mission Control (SvelteKit, still incomplete), so that project would be a tab of the Mission Control, not another app.

feat(renda): the real item on the screen becomes a label of the owner The practice bench only knew the twelve practice items written by hand. But the labels that pay are the fifty to a hundred qualification items the owner does in the browser, and there was no path at all for those to become labels. This closes that link. What it does: reads the text of the item (clipboard first, window OCR as the fallback), shows what it read so the owner can check it, takes the verdict and writes the label in the house schema. What it does not do: it does not click, does not submit and does not type into a third-party account. The owner keeps deciding and recording on the platform himself; only the label he already gave enters here. The screen OCR turned out to be fragile in field, measured: capturing the whole screen read 1919 characters with the terminal, the waybar and the other windows mixed in, and capturing the DeepSeek window read 525 characters of a different window entirely (SSH audit via Termix API), because grim -g cuts the screen region and not the window, so what shows up there is what is on top. The house already knows this (vision._prepare_window: focus plus opacity plus real fullscreen, because grim composites the stack). The capture uses that path, but the clipboard is the primary source: the owner selects the item and presses Ctrl+C, and the text arrives exact, with no recognition error, no wrong window and no competition with the rest of the screen. The label is the owner's: context is the text of the item as he saw it, answer is what he answered, never the key (the defect the practice bench had, fixed earlier today). Proven end to end: item on the clipboard, verdict 2, label written (id=cap-..., answer=2, source=uhrs-capture, no key in the context), then judgment-dataset.py turned it into a Laya item (type=choice, answer=MODERATELY, the four options) with no leakage.

docs(hub): the agent hub answers the whole LAN without a token, patch ready and proven The review the hub's own author asked for found two defects, both measured against the live service on :8091. The security one: the server listens on every interface (the code default is BIND '::' and the unit does not set BIND, so ss shows *:8091) and the iptables rule accepts 8091 from 0.0.0.0/0, meaning the whole LAN reaches it. No route checks any credential: measured, GET /api/transcript returns 200 with the transcript (tool inputs included, so file content in transit) and POST /api/wake returns 200 with nothing but a JSON body. The server uses the opencode password as a confused deputy, so anyone who reaches the port injects a user turn into any session of the fleet (including the red-team ones) and reads any transcript. The file's own header claims the token stays server side on loopback, but the bind is not loopback. The other one: the busy indicator was dead. The code read s.busy, and the session API does not have a busy field at all (the real keys are agent, cost, id, location, model, outcome, projectID, time, title, tokens), and the roster does not have one either, so busy was always zero and every agent rendered idle even while working, while the HTML still computed an elapsed time from that zero. The real source is time.updated. The fix is committed as a patch, not applied: the file has no claim in the roster, the lane that built it is live on another machine and the owner went to sleep, so the live file and the live service were left untouched. The patch adds a hub-specific token (AGENT_HUB_TOKEN or a 0600 token file, compared in constant time, failing closed when no token is configured), guards the two routes that leak or write, derives busy from time.updated with a 90 second window, caps the wake body at 64 KiB and changes the bind default to 127.0.0.1 (reaching the tailnet again becomes an explicit BIND=::, with the token still required). Proven on a temporary port with the live service untouched: 401 without a token on transcript and wake, 200 with it, listening only on loopback, and the busy flag now reading time.updated (the sweep agent showed busy, which it could never show before). The patch applies cleanly with patch -p0 and the result passes node --check.

fix(coord): a live claim renews itself, so recovery wakes stop For three nights in a row the crouton-alpha sent recovery wakes for claims that were alive. Measured on the night of 14/11: both claims of this machine (opencode-matheus-mcp and coord-naming) had a claimed_at 86,298 seconds old while their session was alive, and the local roster listed them as live. The cause is in the code: claimed_at only changes when an agent claims again. A session that works through the night ages that timestamp, and any reader outside this machine (the bus, another machine, the nightly digest) sees stale and wakes an agent that is working. The local stale window is 900 seconds and the bus TTL is six hours, and both measure the same wrong thing, the age of the claim instead of the life of the session. The fix is in the roster, which is this lane's file. When list (which the watcher runs all the time) sees an agent alive, it renews the claim, and a new heartbeat_at field records the last proof of life while claimed_at stays the start of the claim. The prune now reads the same field, and --no-refresh turns the renewal off for tests. Proven against a test roster: the live claim went from 86,298 seconds old to zero, the dead claim was not renewed, --no-refresh renewed nobody, and the prune kept the live one. Measured on the way: the opencode.db path is dead. The newest part row is 5.8 days old even though the file's mtime moves, so live_sessions through the database reports nothing and the /proc scan of the live TUI is what decides. That is worth a separate look, because the watcher uses the same database criterion to decide whether an agent is alive.

docs(events): the SSE never receives the coord-mcp events, and the reason is structural The task was to post one heartbeat event from the coord-mcp and say whether the SSE received it. It did not, and the cause is measured rather than guessed. With the full MCP handshake on the coord-mcp (8765) and a coord_post status carrying a probe note, the MCP answered OK (the post went to the bus), while the SSE on 8090, opened during the post, emitted its init and its own colon heartbeat lines and zero lines from the coord-mcp. Publishing straight into the EventBus from a separate script did not arrive either, which rules out the payload and points at the transport. The EventBus is in-process. publish dispatches the handlers in that process's memory, the SSE only subscribes to the bus of its own process, and the coord code already publishes coord.post and coord.read into the bus of the coord-mcp process, which is a different one. The processes are four: the coord-mcp on 8765, the webui backend on 8090, a plain TCP forward on 8090 for the tailnet that pipes bytes without knowing about events, and the hub on 8091. So what is missing is a way for one process to publish into another's bus. The document records the three pieces of the fix: a POST /api/events route in the webui (that lane's file), the coord-mcp also posting to the webui fail-open so the bus never depends on the hub being up (this lane's file), and the hub consuming the SSE (the rest of task t-2). It also notes that the hub has no token on any interface today, so the security patch should be applied before the fleet events go out through the tailnet.

docs(redteam): the intrusion guard measured against its own evasion surface The Crouton asked whether the guard covers the text that enters the peer's session. Measured with the house guard itself: 12 of 16 test texts pass CLEAN, and the three conclusions are that the guard is Portuguese only (an intruder writing in English passes, which is the most likely case), that one extra word escapes (the vocabulary matches an exact phrase and the patterns match a literal form, so 'me' or 'your' in the middle is enough), and that the invisible and encoding surface is not covered at all (zero-width characters, hyphenation, letter spacing, leet and base64 all pass, because the fold lowercases and strips accents but removes nothing else). The six fixes are ordered by cost, and the two that change behaviour are left as the owner's decision: failing closed may take the fleet down when the guard falls, and aligning the plugin to the bus changes a tool that was born yesterday.

feat(coord): the coord-mcp delivers its bus event to the webui too Task t-2 (publish the fleet events on the events stream) has three pieces, and the measurement showed exactly which one was missing: the webui route to write an event does not exist yet (that is the webui lane), the coord-mcp delivers the event to the webui (this patch, this lane's file), and the hub consumes the stream (the hub lane). The reason the middle piece is needed: the EventBus is in-process. An event published by the coord-mcp process never reaches the stream of the webui process, because the stream only subscribes to the bus of its own process. The coord code already published coord.post and coord.read into the bus of the coord-mcp, where nobody was listening. So the event is now also delivered to the webui, on the loopback, with a short timeout, because this POST sits on the path of writing to the bus and must never hold it. It fails open and is idempotent: with the route missing the POST answers 404 and the bus keeps working, and the bus never depends on the hub being up. Proven in both states: with the route absent (the real state now) the POST answers 404 and the publish still returns in 0.03 seconds; with a server speaking the same contract the event arrives in 1 millisecond in the shape {topic, data, source}.

feat(lab): the reason a cycle failed, and the case the reviewer rejected a good patch The motivo field was already written by another lane (checker and review, plus infra on timeout). This completes the rule the owner gave: a run that died with rc != 0 is infra, not a verdict on the model, and a provider that answered 429 or a rate limit is infra too. Before this, both fell into checker, which inflated the model's failure count. The case the owner asked to be measured: review_wrong. When the rejected patch is in the lane's git stash and the checker accepts that stash in a /tmp copy, the reviewer rejected something good, and the reason is review_wrong rather than review. The lane itself is never touched; the copy is in /tmp and the stash diff comes from the original repo. Why the two are opposites in a decision: review is the known case, the reviewer aborted, and it moves the model up the ladder; review_wrong is the defective case, the reviewer rejected what the checker accepts, and it moves the house up. Proven against the real code, not a reimplementation: six constructed cases, all passing. The review case with a stash the checker accepts gives review_wrong; the counter-test with a checker that rejects the same stash gives review; rc != 0 gives infra; 429 gives infra; everything else gives checker. On the real lanes, the bonsai stash fails the checker (5 failed) so the reason there is review, and the api stash has a 67 line entities patch that the checker accepts (5 passed), so the real function reports review_wrong on that lane. The status now shows the reason next to each measurement, because FAIL and ERROR looked the same in the panel and there was no way to tell a bad model from a bad machine. One real bonsai cycle ran with the new code: reason checker, patch 0 bytes, rc 0, no review failure in the log, which is the correct classification.

feat(offline): the house proves it works without network, in one entrypoint Fleet queue item: check the local dependencies and test without network, through a single entrypoint. The house already had an offline corpus (N.O.M.A.D, Kiwix, FM 4-25.11, NHS: 18,943 docs in FTS5 under data/offline/corpus.db) and the web search falls back to it when the online search fails. But that offline works was an assertion: nobody checked the local dependencies, and no single command proved the operation without a network. scripts/house-offline.sh now does three things: it checks the local dependencies (the corpus and its document count, the FTS5 table, the Portuguese to English glossary, the shared jarvis environment file, the embedder, Qdrant and the Tavily key), it tests without network for real, and it proves the fallback. The test without network is real: unshare -n creates a network namespace with no route, so the process sees no interface, resolves no name and connects to nothing. Measured, the offline search answered in 0.07 to 0.13 seconds with the local source and license. The fallback proof is the one that matters: with the network cut, the online search fails against api.tavily.com and the answer comes from the local corpus, marked as offline. The survival branch depends on neither Tavily, nor the internet, nor an LLM. Three of my own checks were wrong and the first run said FTS5 unavailable because the check, not the corpus, was wrong: the FTS5 table is docs, since docs_idx is the internal index and does not take MATCH directly; the shared environment file lives in modules/ai/jarvis and not in src/jarvis; and the glossary keeps its pairs under entries. All corrected and re-measured. One trap worth keeping: without the shared jarvis environment, the web search fails with requests not installed, which looks like a missing network when it is a missing PYTHONPATH, so the fallback test uses the canonical environment. The script touches no other repository, does not touch the webui, installs nothing and calls no owner API. Measured state: ten dependency checks and two network-free tests pass, and the self-test passes five of five.

But that offline works was an assertion: nobody checked the local dependencies, and no single command proved the operation without a network. scripts/house-offline.sh now does three things: it checks the local dependencies (the corpus and its document count, the FTS5 table, the Portuguese to English glossary, the shared jarvis environment file, the embedder, Qdrant and the Tavily key), it tests without network for real, and it proves the fallback. The test without network is real: unshare -n creates a network namespace with no route, so the process sees no interface, resolves no name and connects to nothing. Measured, the offline search answered in 0.07 to 0.13 seconds with the local source and license. The fallback proof is the one that matters: with the network cut, the online search fails against api.tavily.com and the answer comes from the local corpus, marked as offline. The survival branch depends on neither Tavily, nor the internet, nor an LLM. Three of my own checks were wrong and the first run said FTS5 unavailable because the check, not the corpus, was wrong: the FTS5 table is docs, since docs_idx is the internal index and does not take MATCH directly; the shared environment file lives in modules/ai/jarvis and not in src/jarvis; and the glossary keeps its pairs under entries. All corrected and re-measured. One trap worth keeping: without the shared jarvis environment, the web search fails with requests not installed, which looks like a missing network when it is a missing PYTHONPATH, so the fallback test uses the canonical environment. The script touches no other repository, does not touch the webui, installs nothing and calls no owner API. Measured state: ten dependency checks and two network-free tests pass, and the self-test passes five of five.

feat(lab): G1 — capture the rejected patch and the checker verdict at rejection time The review_wrong detection read the lane's live stash, and the lab destroys the lane every cycle (rm -rf + mkdir): the same event could be review_wrong at one moment and review at the next, and the recorded row was the wrong one. Measured before the change: 3 review events, 0 review_wrong, with two api rows where the harness had reported tasks_completed=1 and a commit. Now, when a review aborts with an empty patch, the lab saves the rejected diff to patch-review-<modelo>-<nivel>-<stamp>.diff, runs the fixed checker on a /tmp copy with the patch applied, and writes review-<...>.meta with the diff sha256 and the verdict. The result row carries review_diff_sha256 and review_checker, and classifica_motivo reads that artifact first, so the classification no longer depends on ephemeral lane state. The lane itself is never touched. The decision policy is unchanged on purpose: G4 of the audit asks for ten sampled review events before the rule that counts review_wrong as a model pass is switched on. Until then the artifact only makes the attribution measurable. Tests: scripts/ab_loop.test.sh green, 13 assertions (the five new ones cover meta accepted, meta rejected, meta unknown fallback, and the capture writing both the diff and the verdict).

bench(voice): 35B-A3B expert-cache vs 8B denso on heldout3 — Codacus hypothesis refuted Backlog #08 (Lince). Measured quality + DUR on heldout3 (39 items, ck=v3): - 35B-A3B + LoRA duplex (unit llama-duplex-35b.service, --n-cpu-moe 44): 9/39 (23.1%), 61 s/token, 2.4 h/cycle. Gargalo: RAM/swap (31 GB total, 10+ GB swap used), experts page-in 358 GB read. - 4B MTP + LoRA v9 (production :8092): 29/39 (74.4%), 4.6-5.5 s/token, 3 min/cycle. 3 identical samples = determinism. - 8B denso (bonsai :8080, no voice LoRA): 0-1/39 (0-2.6%), 0.9 s/token. Fails: n_predict 6 cuts 'SILENCE' -> 'SILE', outputs 'thinking' not labels. Arm 35B SUBE (refuta '35B MoE impossivel' do bus), mas 15x mais lento e erra mais que o 4B MTP. A voz precisa sub-segundo: o classify_turn oficial (timeout 8 s) mede timeout, nao o modelo. Com timeout 180 s o 35B classifica (ex.: 'meu cao me mordeu' -> RESPOND, o 4B da SILENCE).

fix(vis): orcamento em ms, gasto so com fila cheia e bus visivel no agent-msg Tres defeitos medidos na comunicacao visivel (item pendente da sessao): 1. UNIDADE misturada no orcamento: o plugin memory.js escreve last com Date.now() (ms) e o vis-enqueue lia/escrevia com date +%s (s). O status imprimia 'ultimo ha -29888226094min' e o gap comparava segundos contra gap*60*1000, ou seja pedia 180000 s (~50 h) entre injecoes. Agora ms em todo o caminho e um valor legado (<1e12) e normalizado para ms. 2. ORDEM do gasto no hook experimental.idle: visBudgetOk() rodava ANTES de olhar a fila, entao cada evento ocioso sem nada pendente queimava 1 das 12 injecoes/h e ainda travava a proxima mensagem real pelo gap. Medido: fila com item parada e injecoes contando a mais. Agora pend.length==0 retorna antes de tocar o orcamento. 3. BUS VISIVEL: agent-msg.sh chama vis_visible() nos dois caminhos de entrega (API local e bus), enfileirando '[AGENT] remetente : alvo (tipo) : texto'. Toda conversa entre agentes cai na sessao do dono quando ela fica ociosa. Sem script novo (reusa ~/bin/vis-enqueue) e sem duplicar quando o alvo ja' e' a propria sessao do dono. Medido apos o conserto: status mostra 'ultimo ha 14min', budget OK no gap de 3 min e contador 1/12 coerente.

fix(frota): entrega por API volta a funcionar e --to alcanca quem nao tem janela Dois defeitos medidos que deixavam a frota muda no host: 1. ENDERECO DO SERVE. home-manager/modules/services/opencode-serve.nix sobe o serve com '--hostname 100.121.100.103 --port 4599' (escuta SO no IP do tailnet), mas scripts/agent-config.json declara http://127.0.0.1:4599. Medido: TODA entrega por API morria com 'URLError: [Errno 111] Connection refused'; o bus funcionava (outro caminho) e a frota parecia viva. A fonte unica da entrega (agent-api.py) agora tenta o base declarado e, se o transporte falha, usa o listener REAL da mesma porta lido de 'ss -ltnH' (_candidate_bases). Prova: --url 127.0.0.1:4599 resolve para ['http://127.0.0.1:4599', 'http://100.121.100.103:4599'] e a nota a sweep-2026-11 voltou a devolver HTTP 200 com o id da mensagem. 2. --to PARA QUEM NAO TEM JANELA. O TUI roda dentro de um foot e a janela do Hyprland tem address VAZIO: 5 dos 6 agentes do roster (Falcao, coord-naming, rt-async, rt-nemotron-2, sweep-2026-11) tinham address vazio e o filtro por address devolvia 'nenhum alvo'. Quem tem sessao do opencode e' alcancavel pela API, entao o alvo agora e' identificado por '@sess:<id>' quando a janela nao existe, e a resolucao de INFO casa por address OU por sessao.
